objective: Design and implement branching strategies for the source code
stem: A team wants short-lived branches merged into `main` at least daily, with `main` always releasable. Which strategy is this?

options.text: Trunk-based development with short-lived feature branches
GitFlow with develop, release and hotfix branches
A long-lived branch per environment
A fork per developer, merged at the end of each sprint

explanation: Trunk-based development keeps branches alive for hours or a day, so merges stay small and integration problems surface immediately. It is the strategy continuous delivery assumes, usually paired with feature flags for work that is not ready to be seen.

whyWrong.B: GitFlow's long-lived develop and release branches deliberately delay integration.
whyWrong.C: Environment branches cause drift and merge conflicts between environments.
whyWrong.D: Forks with sprint-end merges are the opposite of daily integration.

stem: Which branch policy setting stops a pull request being completed until the linked build succeeds?

options.text: A build validation policy set to required
A minimum number of reviewers
A comment resolution requirement
A merge strategy restriction

explanation: Build validation queues the pipeline against the merged result and blocks completion until it passes. Set to optional it still runs but does not block, which is a useful way to introduce a new check without breaking everyone's flow.

whyWrong.B: Reviewer counts gate on people, not on a build.
whyWrong.C: Comment resolution requires discussions to be closed.
whyWrong.D: Merge strategy controls the shape of the resulting history.

stem: Certain files must be reviewed by the security team whenever they change, automatically, on every pull request. What implements this?

options.text: An automatically included reviewers policy scoped to those file paths
A required build validation on those files
A branch lock on the paths
A repository-level permission denying others write access

explanation: Azure Repos can add specific reviewers automatically when a pull request touches matching paths, and make them required. GitHub's equivalent is a `CODEOWNERS` file combined with required review from code owners.

whyWrong.B: A build cannot represent a human security review.
whyWrong.C: Locks block pushes entirely rather than routing review.
whyWrong.D: Denying write access stops the change being proposed at all.

stem: A repository has grown to several gigabytes because designers commit large binary assets. What is the appropriate fix?

options.text: Move the binaries to Git LFS so only pointers are stored in history
Add the binaries to `.gitignore` and share them over a file share
Run `git gc --aggressive` on the server
Shallow-clone the repository in every pipeline

explanation: Git stores a complete new object for every version of a binary, so history grows without bound. LFS keeps a small pointer in the repository and the content in separate storage, which keeps clones fast while the assets remain versioned.

whyWrong.B: Ignoring them removes version control from files the team clearly needs versioned.
whyWrong.C: Garbage collection reclaims unreferenced objects; reachable history is unaffected.
whyWrong.D: Shallow clones speed up builds but leave the repository just as large for humans.

docs.title: Manage large files with Git LFS

stem: A monolithic repository is being split so each team owns its own repo, but one shared library must remain usable from both. What is the cleanest approach?

options.text: Publish the shared library as a versioned package to an Azure Artifacts feed
Add the shared library as a Git submodule in each repository
Copy the library source into both repositories
Keep the library in the monolith and have teams branch from it

explanation: Packaging gives consumers an explicit, versioned dependency, so each team upgrades when it suits them and the contract is visible. This is the standard answer when a repository split needs shared code.

whyWrong.B: Submodules work but pin a commit rather than a version, and are notoriously easy to leave stale.
whyWrong.C: Copies diverge immediately and fixes have to be applied twice.
whyWrong.D: That defeats the point of splitting the monolith.

stem: A password was committed six months ago and the commit is deep in history. What must happen?

options.text: Rotate the credential immediately, then purge it from history and force-push the rewritten branch
Delete the file in a new commit and enable secret scanning
Purge it from history, which makes rotation unnecessary
Make the repository private and leave history intact

explanation: Rotation comes first and matters most: anyone who cloned the repository still holds the secret, and history rewriting cannot reach those copies. Purging history is worth doing afterwards to stop it spreading further.

whyWrong.B: Deleting the file leaves the secret in every earlier commit.
whyWrong.C: This has the order backwards — a leaked secret must be treated as compromised.
whyWrong.D: Restricting access does nothing about clones already taken.

docs.title: Remove sensitive data from a repository

stem: Which pull request merge strategy produces a single commit on the target branch, discarding the individual commits from the source branch?

options.text: Squash merge
Merge (no fast-forward)
Rebase and fast-forward
Semi-linear merge

explanation: Squash collapses the branch into one commit on the target, which keeps `main` readable at the cost of losing the individual steps. Rebase replays each commit onto the tip, preserving them in a linear history.

whyWrong.B: A no-fast-forward merge keeps every source commit plus a merge commit.
whyWrong.C: Rebase replays each commit individually onto the target.
whyWrong.D: Semi-linear rebases then creates a merge commit, keeping the individual commits.

stem: Order the steps of a governed change reaching `main` in a trunk-based repository.

options.text: Create a short-lived branch from main
Open a pull request, which triggers build validation
Required reviewers approve and all comments are resolved
Complete the pull request, merging into main
Delete the source branch

explanation: The gates run before the merge, not after — that is the whole point of a branch policy. Deleting the branch on completion keeps the repository tidy and can be set as the default in Azure Repos.

stem: Which file makes GitHub request review from a named team whenever files under `/infra` change?

options.text: `CODEOWNERS`
`.gitattributes`
`dependabot.yml`
`.github/pull_request_template.md`

explanation: `CODEOWNERS` maps path patterns to owning users or teams, and combined with the branch protection rule requiring review from code owners it becomes a hard gate rather than a suggestion.

whyWrong.B: `.gitattributes` controls line endings, diff behaviour and LFS tracking.
whyWrong.D: A template pre-fills the pull request description.
